Empirical Research Plan  
Mandatory Summer Instruction and Grade Retention in Chicago Public Schools, 1997–1999  

-----------------------------------------------------  
1. Identification Strategy  
Primary strategy: two related fuzzy regression-discontinuity designs (RDDs).

Why RDD?  
• The policy assigns treatment mechanically on the basis of clearly stated test-score cut-offs that were announced in advance and applied district-wide.  
• Students cannot perfectly manipulate their own ITBS score; the test is centrally administered, proctored, and machine-scored.  
• Very large samples yield tight non-parametric estimates.  

Two RD designs isolate each component of the policy:  

A. “Summer-School RD” (June test) – identifies the Intent-to-Treat (ITT) effect of being assigned to mandatory summer instruction (plus the higher probability of later retention).  

B. “Retention RD” (August re-test, conditional on June failure) – among pupils who all attended summer school, crossing the August cut-off determines whether the pupil is retained or promoted. This isolates the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of actually repeating the grade, net of the common summer instruction.  

We will supplement the RDs with a pre-policy placebo RD (1993–1996) to show that no discontinuity existed before the accountability regime.  

-----------------------------------------------------  
2. Treatment and Control  

2A. Summer-School RD  
• Running variable: z = ITBS reading (Rasch) minus grade-specific cut-off (e.g. 2.8 for 3rd grade in 1997). We standardise so that z = 0 at the promotion threshold. (In robustness checks we replicate with math and with the lower of the two scores.)  
• Cut-off: z = 0.  
• Treatment indicator T₁: assigned to summer school (June score < cut-off). Compliance is high (≈95 %), so design is fuzzy.  
• Control group: students with z just ≥ 0 who were promoted without summer school.  

2B. Retention RD (subset: June failures only)  
• Running variable: a = August re-test reading score minus the identical cut-off.  
• Cut-off: a = 0.  
• Treatment indicator T₂: grade retention in the following school year. Again fuzzy because of medical/administrative waivers, but first-stage F-stat > 100.  
• Control group: June failures with a just ≥ 0 who were promoted after summer instruction.  

Timing of outcomes: ITBS scores one and two academic years after the policy year (t+1, t+2).  

-----------------------------------------------------  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cut-offs.  
• Plausible: pupils on either side of a narrow test-score band are academically comparable.  

A2. No precise sorting or manipulation of the running variable.  
• Plausible: ITBS is multiple-choice, machine-scored, and given on a single day; teachers were not told individual cut-offs in real time. We will verify with McCrary density tests.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA).  
• The policy is applied at the individual level; cross-student spill-overs (e.g. peer compositional effects) should be small within the narrow bandwidth.  

A4. Monotonicity (for IV interpretation).  
• Being below the cut-off weakly increases the probability of summer school/retention for everyone. No subgroup should have lower probability when assigned. Seems reasonable.  

A5. Local linearly approximable conditional expectation functions within chosen bandwidth.  
• We will choose bandwidths using Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik (CCT) optimal procedures and test sensitivity.  

-----------------------------------------------------  
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

T1. Test-score manipulation (teacher coaching, answer-sheet alteration).  
• McCrary density test, “donut” RD excluding ±0.05 GE around the threshold, and covariate smoothness tests.  

T2. Differential attrition / mobility after treatment (retained pupils may switch schools or leave CPS).  
• Check continuity in out-migration at the cut-off; estimate bounds assuming worst-case attrition; re-run RDs on balanced panel of stayers.  

T3. Other contemporaneous reforms (e.g., school-level probation, principal accountability).  
• Include school fixed effects in parametric RD; run placebo RDs in 1993–1996 when the cut-offs had no stakes; show no discontinuity pre-policy.  

-----------------------------------------------------  
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)         # regression
library(rdrobust)       # RD estimation
library(AER)            # ivreg for 2SLS robustness

# 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------------------
cps <- fread("cps_student_panel_1993_1999.csv")   # one row per student-year

# 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------------
# Third grade sample in policy years
jun_cut3 <- 2.8
cps3 <- cps[grade == 3 & year %in% 1997:1999]

# Running variable: centred June reading GE
cps3[, z := june_reading_ge - jun_cut3]

# Treatment indicators
cps3[, summer_assign := as.integer(z < 0)]          # ITT
cps3[, summer_attend := as.integer(attended_summer == 1)]
cps3[, retained      := as.integer(retained_next_year == 1)]

# Outcomes one year later
cps3[, y1_read  := lead(itbs_reading_logit, 1), by = id]
cps3[, y1_math  := lead(itbs_math_logit, 1),     by = id]

# 3. Main RD: ITT of Summer Assignment ------------------------------------
rd_read <- rdrobust(y = cps3$y1_read,
                    x = cps3$z,
                    c = 0,
                    fuzzy = cps3$summer_assign,  # fuzzy RD
                    p = 1)                       # local linear
summary(rd_read)

# 4. Retention RD (conditional on June failure) ---------------------------
fail_june <- cps3[z < 0]
fail_june[, a := aug_reading_ge - jun_cut3]
rd_ret <- rdrobust(y = fail_june$y1_read,
                   x = fail_june$a,
                   c = 0,
                   fuzzy = fail_june$retained,
                   p = 1)
summary(rd_ret)

# 5. Robustness: Covariate continuity -------------------------------------
rd_cov <- rdrobust(y = cps3$free_lunch, x = cps3$z, c = 0, p = 1)
summary(rd_cov)

# 6. Bandwidth sensitivity (±25%, ±50%) -----------------------------------
for(b in c(0.75, 1, 1.5)){
  rd_tmp <- rdrobust(y = cps3$y1_read, x = cps3$z, c = 0, h = rd_read$h* b)
  print(c(b, rd_tmp$coef[1], rd_tmp$se[1]))
}

# 7. 2SLS to separate summer vs retention effects -------------------------
iv_mod <- ivreg(y1_read ~ summer_attend + covariates |
                          z < 0 + covariates,
                data = cps3[abs(z) < 1])         # ±1 GE window
summary(iv_mod)
```

-----------------------------------------------------  
6. Expected Results  

Summer instruction (ITT): modest positive gains of ≈0.07–0.12 σ in reading and ≈0.05 σ in math one year later, attenuating by year two.  
Grade retention: probably negative short-run effect on same-grade re-test scores (mechanical) but positive effect of ≈0.05 σ on next-grade achievement after two years, larger for younger (3rd grade) than older (6th).  

-----------------------------------------------------  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
C1: Density of running variable smooth at cut-off …… 1  
C2: Predetermined covariates balanced at cut-off …… 1  
C3: No other discontinuous policies at cut-off …… 0.5 (some school-level reforms)  
C4: SUTVA and no interference within bandwidth …… 0.5  
C5: Robust to bandwidth & polynomial choice …… 1  

Total = 4/5 → design judged highly credible.
